raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old male, with known alcoholic cirrhosis for the past 6 years, was admitted for persisting evening fever and abdominal dilatation. The patient abstained from alcohol since diagnosis and had a history of esophageal variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy episodes, and ascites development in the past but had been ascites-free for at least 6 months prior to admission. His medical history also included insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. He continued to work as a confectioner. On admission, clinical evaluation and subsequent imaging demonstrated massive ascites and splenomegaly, with no signs of portal thrombosis. Laboratory evaluation showed mild pancytopenia and increase C-reactive protein (CRP), while other biochemistry markers were, in general, normal. Numerous cultures were drawn from multiple sites, including bone marrow, and serology tests for various pathogens were performed. Cultures were positive for B. melitensis, a diagnosis further confirmed by real time-polymerase chain reaction (PCR based on direct amplification of a 207-base pair DNA sequence of a gene specific for the Brucella genus, BCSP31) and agglutination (Rose Bengal plate agglutination test), Wright seroagglutination test, and ELISA serology (Serion ELISA IgG/IgM/IgA antibodies to Brucella melitensis). The patient retrospectively admitted to consuming unpasteurized dairy products (sheep and goats) 2 months prior to admission.
Initiation of antibiotic therapy was problematic since there was a vague history of tetracycline intolerance in the past, and the underlying pathology advocated against the use of the hepatotoxic doxycycline and rifampicin and the potentially hepatorenal syndrome inducers, aminoglycosides. The remaining options were trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily, which were initiated as soon as diagnosis was confirmed. Defervescence was indeed achieved on day 5, albeit accompanied by renal function disorders, with a gradual increase in serum creatinine up to 2 mg/dl, with normal values (nv) of 0.6-1.2 mg/dl. On day 12, fever relapsed, accompanied by worsening pancytopenia and renal function values. Extensive diagnostic workup was performed, including further cultures and imaging and excluding any other underlying infection, and it was decided to substitute cotrimoxazole with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, since the benefit of brucellosis therapy overruled the risk of doxycycline-hepatotoxicity at that point. Defervescence was achieved 8 days later, accompanied by partial reversal of renal function and pancytopenia. The patient was successfully discharged and referred to a transplantation center for further evaluation. Forty days after doxycycline-ciprofloxacin initiation, the patient was readmitted due to hepatic encephalopathy, worsening of ascites and pancytopenia, and low-grade fever: any underlying cause was excluded through a scrutinized workup and supportive measures initiation. Doxycycline was discontinued as a potential inducer of decompensation, and the patient was transferred to a transplantation center.
Since pulmonary hypertension had been detected, the patient was not considered a candidate for liver transplantation and he continued to rapidly deteriorate until the adverse outcome.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male with alcoholic cirrhosis presented with persisting evening fever and progressive abdominal dilatation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been abstinent from alcohol for 6 years and ascites-free for at least 6 months, presented with persisting evening fever and abdominal dilatation. After admission, defervescence was initially achieved on day 5 of antimicrobial therapy but was complicated by acute renal impairment. On hospital day 12, fever relapsed with worsening pancytopenia and renal dysfunction, prompting a regimen adjustment that achieved defervescence 8 days later. Forty days after antibiotic initiation, he was readmitted with recurrent low-grade fever, hepatic encephalopathy, worsening ascites, and pancytopenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Alcoholic cirrhosis diagnosed 6 years prior (abstinent since diagnosis) with prior esophageal variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, and ascites (ascites-free for at least 6 months prior to admission); insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; pulmonary hypertension; vague history of tetracycline intolerance. Epidemiological exposure: Retrospectively reported consuming unpasteurized sheep and goat dairy products 2 months prior to admission. Occupation: Confectioner.
subjective.review_of_systems: Allergies/Intolerances: Vague history of tetracycline intolerance in the past. Other review of systems not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Massive ascites and splenomegaly. Readmission (day 40): Hepatic encephalopathy, low-grade fever, and marked abdominal ascites.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline labs: Mild pancytopenia; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP); other biochemical markers generally normal. Follow-up labs: Gradual increase in serum creatinine up to 2 mg/dl (normal values 0.6-1.2 mg/dl) on day 5; worsening pancytopenia and elevated renal function indices on day 12; partial reversal of renal function and pancytopenia following medication change. Readmission: Worsening pancytopenia.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal imaging: Massive ascites and splenomegaly, with no signs of portal thrombosis. Bone marrow sampling: Aspiration performed for microbiological evaluation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis confirmed by positive cultures from multiple sites including bone marrow yielding Brucella melitensis, further verified by real-time PCR targeting the 207-bp BCSP31 gene specific for Brucella genus, Rose Bengal plate agglutination test, Wright seroagglutination test, and Serion ELISA serology (IgG/IgM/IgA antibodies to Brucella melitensis). Underlying infections excluded on repeat diagnostic workups.
Plan & Clinical Course: Initially treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily and ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily (doxycycline, rifampicin, and aminoglycosides initially avoided due to hepatotoxicity/hepatorenal risks and tetracycline intolerance history). Defervescence achieved on day 5 but complicated by nephrotoxicity (creatinine 2 mg/dl). On day 12, fever and cytopenias relapsed; trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was substituted with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Defervescence occurred 8 days later with clinical improvement and discharge. Forty days post-initiation, readmitted with decompensated cirrhosis (hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, cytopenias, low-grade fever); doxycycline was stopped. Patient transferred to a transplantation center, but deemed ineligible due to pulmonary hypertension and experienced rapid deterioration resulting in death.
